newsitem.title: USA: Government unveils new merger guidelines.
newsitem.headline: Government unveils new merger guidelines.

text.p: Government trustbusters released long-awaited guidelines Tuesday, outlining their criteria for judging claims that mergers should pass muster because they will increase efficiencies.
Federal Trade Commission Chairman Robert Pitofsky is a strong advocate of considering potential efficiencies as an argument for approving mergers among firms that compete in the same market.
But the updated guidelines make clear some kinds of efficiencies will be much tougher to prove than others when companies want to unite.

The guidelines arrived on the eve of the spring meeting of the American Bar Association antitrust section in Washington, so they are certain to be a talking point among one of their intended audiences -- the hundreds of antitrust lawyers who descend on Washington Wednesday for their annual three-day meeting.

The guidelines issued by the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division are not meant to have the force of law. Instead, they give government staffers and the public a clearer look at the thinking of regulators.

"There are a number of audiences here," said Lawrence Fullerton, the Justice Department antitrust division's deputy assistant attorney general for mergers. He said the guidelines are for government staff as well as for lawyers representing merging parties.

Companies proposing to combine almost always argue that their mergers will increase efficiency. The four-page document issued Tuesday, revising a portion of horizontal merger guidelines issued five years ago, explain when such arguemnts are most likely to carry weight.
One question government regulators will ask is whether efficiencies enhance a merged firm's capacity to behave competitively, leading to higher quality, better service, lower prices or new products.
If a proposed merger passes that test, then the government will look more closely at the claims of efficiencies.
"Certain types of efficiencies are more likely to be cognizable and substantial than others," the guidelines say.

To demonstrate what it is talking about, the government indicated that quantifiable efficiencies -- perhaps the shifting of production facilities once owned separately to cut production costs -- are among the strongest candidates for consideration.
But efficiencies that are slightly harder to quantify, such as the effect of research and development, may not be as seriously considered.
And others -- possible examples given in the guidelines are management, procurement and capital cost efficiencies -- may be the toughest to prove.
One antitrust lawyer welcomed the guidelines as useful for everyone practicing in the field. But he said there will still be many questions.

"It sounds so simple," said Richard Steuer of Kaye, Scholer in New York. "They're saying you can measure the dollar effect of the efficiencies and you can measure the dimension of the anticompetitive effect on consumers, do the math and consider whether you approve or disapprove. It should only be so easy."
